en: The Parivāra:
The Second Part of the Analysis of the Monks' Rules (Bhikkhuvibhaṅga)
1.10 Section on the Occurrence of Offenses 1.
Chapter on the Defeats (Pārājika):
On account of engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs four offenses:
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is unexposed, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika);
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is mostly exposed, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If he inserts the penis without touching it into a mouth that has been made circular, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if [the mouth] is smeared with resin, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
On account of engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs these four offenses.
How many offenses does one commit by way of taking what is not given?
By way of taking what is not given, one commits three offenses.
If one takes what is not given, valued at five māsakas or more than five māsakas, in the manner of theft, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If one takes what has not been given, by way of theft, with a value of more than one māsaka or less than five māsakas, it is a thullaccaya offense;
if one takes what has not been given, by way of theft, with a value of one māsaka or less than a māsaka, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
On account of taking what has not been given, one incurs these three offenses.
On account of intentionally depriving a human being of life, how many offenses does one commit?
On account of intentionally depriving a human being of life, one commits three offenses:
if one digs a pit aiming at a human being, thinking, "He will fall in and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When the victim falls and painful feeling arises, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
if they die, there is an offense of pārājika.
By intentionally depriving a human being of life, one incurs these three offenses.
How many offenses does one commit by claiming a non-existent, unreal superhuman state?
By reason of claiming a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, one commits three offenses:
if, being of evil desires and driven by longing, one claims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If one says, "The monk who lives in your monastery is an arahant," there is an offense of thullaccaya for one who understands [the claim],
and an offense of dukkaṭa for one who does not understand.
By means of proclaiming a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, one incurs these three offenses.
The four *pārājika* offenses are concluded.
2. The section beginning with the *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
How many offenses does one incur by means of making an effort to emit semen?
By making an effort for the purpose of discharging impurity, one incurs three offenses:
if one intends, makes an effort, and there is discharge, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if one intends and makes an effort, but there is no discharge, it is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
There is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
by reason of making an effort and discharging impurity, one incurs these three offenses.
How many offenses does one incur by reason of engaging in physical contact?
On account of engaging in physical contact, one incurs five offenses:
if a lustful bhikkhunī consents to being grasped by a lustful man below the collarbone and above the knees, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika);
if a bhikkhu touches body with body, it is an offense entailing formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa).
If one touches something connected to the body with the body, it is an offense of thullaccaya;
if one touches something connected to the body with something connected to the body, it is an offense of dukkaṭa;
for poking with a finger, it is a pācittiya.
On account of engaging in physical contact, one incurs these five offenses.
On account of addressing a woman with lewd words, one incurs three offenses:
if, referring to her anus or her vagina, one speaks in praise or speaks in dispraise, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).

Excluding the path for feces and the path for urine, if one speaks in praise or speaks in dispraise with reference to what is below the collarbone and above the knees, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
If one speaks in praise or speaks in dispraise with reference to something connected to the body, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
By reason of speaking in praise of serving one’s own desires, one incurs three offenses.
If he speaks in praise of serving one’s own desires in the presence of a woman, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if he speaks in praise of serving one’s own desires in the presence of a paṇḍaka, it is a serious offense (thullaccaya);
if he speaks in praise of serving one’s own desires in the presence of an animal, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
On account of engaging in matchmaking, one incurs three offenses:
if one accepts the proposal, investigates it, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if one accepts the proposal and investigates it, but does not report back, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If he accepts it but does not examine it and does not return it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
On account of having a hut built by means of a request, one incurs three offenses: while having it built, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the preliminary effort (*payoga*); ... [and so forth].
When one lump [of clay] has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
when that lump has arrived, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
On account of having a large dwelling built, one incurs three offenses:
If he causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
when even one morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
when that morsel has arrived, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
By reason of groundlessly charging a bhikkhu with an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika), one incurs three offenses:
if one speaks with the intention of causing him to leave the Order without having asked for his consent, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if one speaks with the intention of abusing him after having asked for his consent, there is an offense of verbal abuse (*omasavāda*).
By reason of charging a bhikkhu with an offense entailing expulsion on account of some part or mere semblance of a legal issue pertaining to something else, one incurs three offenses:
if, without having asked for leave, one speaks with the intention of causing him to fall away [from the Saṅgha], there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if, after having asked for leave, one speaks with the intention of reviling him, there is an offense of abusive speech (*omasavāda*).
On account of not relinquishing [his position] after being pressed up to three times, a monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha incurs three offenses:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the formal motion (ñatti);
two offenses of grave wrongdoing (thullaccaya) for the two proclamations (kammavācā).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
By reason of not relinquishing [the course of action] after being exhorted up to three times, monks who follow those who cause schism incur three offenses:
an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the motion (*ñatti*).
With two proclamations, there are thullaccaya offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
On account of not relinquishing [his position] after being pressed up to three times, an obstinate monk incurs three offenses:
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for two proclamations of the formal act (kammavācā), there are offenses of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
at the conclusion of the formal act, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
On account of not relinquishing [his behavior] after being pressed up to three times, a monk who corrupts a family incurs three offenses:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the motion (ñatti);
two offenses of grave wrongdoing (thullaccaya) for the two proclamations (kammavācā).

At the conclusion of the formal proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) … [as before] … How many offenses does one commit by reason of voiding excrement, urine, or spittle in water out of disrespect?
By reason of voiding excrement, urine, or spittle in water out of disrespect, one commits one offense.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa):
out of disrespect, by reason of voiding feces, urine, or spittle in water, one incurs this one offense.
The second section on the classification of offenses is finished.
